316.title: Peace with God (Romans 5:1–11)
316.hook: suffering, patience, character, hope; while we were still sinners, Christ died
316.howItsDone: Christians often turn to Romans 5:1–5 in illness or loss; chaplains and friends read it with people in a hard season, and look back together on what that season grew.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was faith, pistis, trust: an old man under the stars. Your line was counted as right.

Ask the steady one in your life how they got that way, the one people call at two in the morning. The answer is rarely: everything went well for me. More often it's: the year my dad was sick. The job I lost. The long winter after the divorce. Something hard happened, and something grew in the hard ground. Nobody chooses the hard part, but what grew is often what they'd keep. Paul knew this from the inside: shipwrecked, beaten, jailed, and still writing letters. In Romans chapter five he traces the pattern step by step, and he starts somewhere surprising: with peace.
screen: `HOW DID THEY GET THAT WAY?` → `SOMETHING HARD HAPPENED.` → `PAUL STARTS WITH PEACE.`

segments.voice: Chapter five opens, in the King James Bible: "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." The Greek word for peace is eirene, and behind it stands the Hebrew shalom: not just no fighting, but wholeness, everything in its right place. After four chapters about guilt and grace, the war is over. Then Paul does something odd. He says we glory, even boast, in tribulations. Not because suffering is good, but because of what can grow in it: "tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed." Four links. Hard times grow endurance. Endurance grows what the King James calls experience; the Greek means tested character, like metal that's been through the fire and proved true. That tested character grows hope, and hope, Paul says, doesn't let you down. Maketh not ashamed echoes Paul's opening a few days ago: not ashamed. Why doesn't it disappoint? Because the love of God has been poured into our hearts. Then the line that holds the chapter up: "But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." Not after we got better. While. Paul notes that hardly anyone would die even for a righteous person. This love didn't wait for anyone to deserve it. Some readers say the chain is easier to see looking back than from the middle of it.
screen: `EIRENE: SHALOM, WHOLENESS.` · `GLORY IN TRIBULATIONS.` · `PATIENCE, TESTED CHARACTER, HOPE.` · `WHILE WE WERE YET SINNERS.` · then, large: `HOPE MAKETH NOT ASHAMED.`

segments.voice: Go back through your life slowly and find one hard season that, looking back, grew something in you: patience, compassion, honesty, a friend you'd never have met. Don't pretend it was good, it may still hurt; just name the hardship and what grew, and if one you're in right now comes instead, let it be there without forcing a lesson on it yet. If you pray, give thanks for what grew, and ask for hope in what hasn't yet.

Your line: hope does not disappoint. The war is over, even in hard ground. Day three hundred sixteen.

317.title: Adam and Christ (Romans 5:12–21)
317.hook: where sin increased, grace abounded all the more
317.howItsDone: Christians read Romans 5 when they teach about sin and salvation, and in the Easter Vigil's ancient hymn, the Exsultet, Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches sing of Adam's fall and of the grace that came after it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was eirene, peace, and the chain from tribulation to hope. Your line was hope does not disappoint.

Some things you inherit without asking. Your grandmother's nose. Your family's way of going quiet when things get tense. A house, or a debt. You didn't choose any of it, and it shapes you anyway. In the second half of Romans chapter five, Paul steps way back from Rome and his own day, all the way to the garden in Genesis. He's thinking about the whole human family and what it has inherited. And he sets two figures side by side, like two ends of a seesaw: the first man, and one more.
screen: `THINGS YOU INHERIT WITHOUT ASKING.` → `BACK TO THE GARDEN.` → `TWO FIGURES, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Paul begins, in the King James Bible: "Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned." One man, Adam, opened a door, and sin and death came through it into the whole human story. Then the other end of the seesaw: "For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous." Adam and Christ. One disobeyed, one obeyed. One brought death, one brings life. But Paul keeps insisting it isn't an even seesaw. Again and again he says much more: the gift is not like the fall. Then the line of the day: "But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound." Paul reaches for a super-word in Greek: grace super-abounded, over-overflowed. However big the mess gets, grace is bigger. Christians understand the Adam side differently. In the West, following Augustine, Catholics and the churches of the Reformation speak of original sin: every person is born sharing in Adam's fallen state, even in some sense his guilt. Orthodox Christians usually speak of ancestral sin: we inherit mortality and a wounded nature, but not Adam's personal guilt. Some scholars trace part of that difference to how one small phrase here was translated into Latin. Either way, Paul's direction is plain. The chapter doesn't end with Adam. It ends with grace reigning, through Jesus Christ.
screen: `BY ONE MAN SIN ENTERED.` · `BY THE OBEDIENCE OF ONE.` · `NOT AN EVEN SEESAW: MUCH MORE.` · `ORIGINAL SIN, ANCESTRAL SIN.` · then, large: `GRACE DID MUCH MORE ABOUND.`

segments.voice: Think of a mistake, yours or someone else's, that turned out smaller than what came after it: a fight that ended in a better friendship, a wrong turn that led somewhere good, someone who forgave you more than you expected. Don't explain it away; just let yourself see that the mistake wasn't the end of the story. If you pray, thank God for that grace, by name.

318.title: Dead to sin (Romans 6)
318.hook: baptism as burial and rising: walk in newness of life
318.howItsDone: Romans 6:3–11 is often read at baptisms and at the Easter Vigil, and some Christians touch water on entering church, or recall their baptism each morning, as a reminder of dying and rising with Christ.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was charis, grace, on Paul's seesaw of Adam and Christ. Your line was grace abounds.

A kid has just been told: whatever you break, it's already forgiven. For a moment the kid looks thoughtful. Then the kid looks at the china cabinet. Paul saw this coming. He's just said that where sin abounded, grace did much more abound, and he can hear someone at the back raising a hand. If more sin means more grace, shouldn't we sin more? Maybe some people in Rome were really asking it. Paul answers with two words, then with a picture of water, a grave and a morning.
screen: `WHATEVER YOU BREAK IS FORGIVEN.` → `SO SHOULD WE SIN MORE?` → `WATER, A GRAVE, A MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the question, in the King James Bible: "What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid." In Greek, me genoito: absolutely not, may it never be. Then baptism. Baptizo means to dip, to plunge under, and Paul says going under the water is like going into a grave: "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life." The old life, run by sin, has been buried. You walk out into a new morning. Dead to sin, for Paul, doesn't mean temptation disappears; it means sin no longer owns you. He talks about slavery, a picture his hearers in Rome saw every day: you used to belong to one master, now you belong to another. And he ends the chapter: "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." Wages are earned. A gift is not. Churches differ. Catholics, Orthodox Christians, and Protestant churches such as Lutherans, Anglicans, Methodists and Presbyterians baptize babies as well as adults, trusting God's grace comes first. Baptists, Pentecostals and others baptize only those old enough to confess faith themselves. Some pour water, some plunge the whole body under, and the Orthodox immerse even infants three times. Romans 6 is often read at baptisms, because the picture is the same: down into the water, up into new life.

319.title: The wretched man (Romans 7:14–25)
319.hook: the good I want, I don't do
319.howItsDone: Christians often turn to Romans 7 when talking honestly about habits and temptation, in confession, in recovery groups and in spiritual direction, where the struggle is named without shame.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was baptizo, a burial and a rising. Your line was newness of life.

The alarm is set for six. The running shoes are by the door. The plan was made with a clear head and good intentions. Then six o'clock comes, and a hand reaches over and turns the alarm off. Or it's the sharp word someone swore they wouldn't say, out loud again. Wanting one thing and doing another is an old, ordinary human knot. The surprise is finding it in Paul's letter to Rome, right after his big picture of new life. He stops arguing, and writes in the first person about a war inside him.
screen: `THE ALARM, THE SHOES, THE SNOOZE.` → `WANTING ONE THING, DOING ANOTHER.` → `PAUL WRITES IN THE FIRST PERSON.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." It doubles back on itself like the knot it describes. Paul says he agrees with God's law. He delights in it. He knows it's good. And still something in him pulls the other way, like a second law at war inside him. The knowing isn't the problem. The doing is. Then the paragraph breaks open into a cry: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" Wretched, talaiporos in Greek, means miserable, worn down by hardship. It isn't a pose; it's a groan. And notice the question. Not how do I fix myself, but who shall deliver me? He's looking outside himself. The answer comes in the very next breath: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord." Now a real puzzle Christians have argued over for a long time: who is this I? Some readers, including Augustine in his later years and Martin Luther, hear the Christian life: even the baptized still feel this war inside, every day. Others, among them early Greek teachers and scholars today, hear life under the law without the Spirit, the way things look before chapter eight. The text doesn't settle it for us. Either way, Paul writes in the present tense, and he doesn't flinch. He doesn't hide the struggle or scold it. He names it, and cries out for help.

320.title: No condemnation (Romans 8:1–17)
320.hook: there is now no condemnation; we cry Abba, Father
320.carry: a child at home, not a prisoner on trial
320.howItsDone: Many Christians memorize Romans 8:1, and many use the word Abba in personal prayer, the way Jesus did in the garden; Romans 8 is often read at baptisms and funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was talaiporos, wretched: the good I want, I don't do. Your line was who shall deliver me?

Some people carry a courtroom around inside their heads, with a prosecutor who never takes a day off. You forgot the birthday: guilty. You snapped at the kids: guilty. That thing from ninth grade: still guilty, somehow, at three in the morning. The case is never closed. Paul ended chapter seven crying out, who shall deliver me? Now he turns the page, and chapter eight, which many readers call the high point of the whole letter, opens with a verdict. And it's very bad news for the prosecutor.
screen: `A COURTROOM INSIDE YOUR HEAD.` → `THE CASE IS NEVER CLOSED.` → `CHAPTER EIGHT OPENS WITH A VERDICT.`

segments.voice: The verdict, in the King James Bible: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus." The Greek word is katakrima, and it's more than a guilty verdict; it's the sentence that follows, the penalty handed down. Not less. None. And not someday: now, an echo of the hinge a few days ago, but now. Then he explains how: the Spirit. In chapter seven the Spirit was hardly mentioned; in chapter eight the Spirit is everywhere, living in people, giving life, leading them. And the courtroom turns into a family room: "For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father." Abba is Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke at home, the word a child uses for a father, close and warm. Mark's Gospel says Jesus himself prayed Abba in the garden the night before he died. Paul keeps it in Aramaic even writing in Greek to Rome, as if some words shouldn't be translated. Adoption was serious in Roman law: an adopted son became a full heir, with a new name and a new standing. And the Spirit itself, Paul says, bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. So the prosecutor doesn't get the last word. A father does. Christians of every church say that doesn't make wrong things right; it means a person isn't defined by them. You can still say sorry, and change. But you do it as a child at home, not as a prisoner on trial.
screen: `KATAKRIMA: THE SENTENCE HANDED DOWN.` · `NOW: NOT SOMEDAY.` · `THE SPIRIT OF ADOPTION.` · `ABBA: A CHILD'S WORD FOR FATHER.` · then, large: `THERE IS THEREFORE NOW NO CONDEMNATION.`

If it comes back, that's all right; set it down again. If you pray, say the old family word, Abba, and rest there.

321.title: Groaning creation (Romans 8:18–27)
321.hook: the whole creation groans in labor; the Spirit prays in groans too deep for words
321.howItsDone: Some Christians lean on Romans 8:26 when they cannot find words, praying in silence, with tears or with a sigh; some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians also connect it with praying in tongues.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was no condemnation, and a family word: Abba, Father. Your line was a child at home, not a prisoner on trial.
screen: `A CHILD AT HOME, NOT A PRISONER ON TRIAL.`

segments.voice: A hospital room, late. Someone sits beside the bed with nothing left to say. Outside, after the bad news, all that comes out is a long breath, not quite a word. Prayer is often pictured as sentences, nicely put, in the right order. Then comes a moment when the sentences are gone. In the middle of Romans chapter eight, Paul stops to talk about exactly that, and he widens it. It isn't only one person who groans, he says. It's the whole world. And then he says something about God and the prayers that have no words.
screen: `A HOSPITAL ROOM, NOTHING TO SAY.` → `A BREATH THAT ISN'T QUITE A WORD.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD GROANS.`

segments.voice: Paul starts honestly: there is suffering now. "For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us." He doesn't deny the suffering; he sets it beside something bigger. Then he turns to the whole created world, oceans, forests, animals, and says it's waiting too. The King James calls it the earnest expectation of the creature: like someone on tiptoe at a window. "For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now." Travaileth means the pains of labor. So the groaning isn't a death rattle; it's a birth. Something new is coming, and the world is in labor with it. Then he brings it home: "Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered." Three groans, then. Creation groans. We groan. And, Paul says, the Spirit of God groans with us, underneath our words, when we have none. That we includes Paul. For him, the prayer doesn't depend on getting the words right. Some Christians say this verse gives them permission to pray with tears, or a sigh, or silence. Some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians connect it with praying in tongues; others read it as the silent prayer of the heart. Both readings find the same promise: nobody groans alone.
screen: `SUFFERING NOW, GLORY COMING.` · `CREATION ON TIPTOE.` · `LABOR PAINS, NOT DEATH PAINS.` · `THE SPIRIT GROANS WITH US.` · then, large: `GROANINGS WHICH CANNOT BE UTTERED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something too big or too tangled for sentences: a person who's sick, the state of the world, something in you that you can't name. Don't explain it; just breathe in and let out one long, slow sigh, then another. If you pray, let the sigh be the prayer, and remember Paul says the Spirit is praying with it; if you don't, let the sighs carry what words can't.
Groaning creation. The whole world in labor pains, waiting for something new, and the Spirit groaning with us, too deep for words.

322.title: All things work together (Romans 8:28–30)
322.hook: for good, to those who love God
322.carry: a good thread in the weave
322.howItsDone: Some Christians hold onto Romans 8:28 in hard seasons, and pastors often explain it carefully so it isn't used to call suffering good.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was groaning creation, and the Spirit praying in sighs too deep for words. Your line was the spirit prays with us.

It shows up on mugs and sympathy cards, and at funerals, said by someone trying to help: everything happens for a reason. Sometimes it lands gently, sometimes like a slap. Tell someone whose child is sick that it's all for a reason, and watch their face. Some people assume the line comes from the Bible. The verse it gets pinned to is in Romans chapter eight, and that verse says something different. So what does it actually say?
screen: `EVERYTHING HAPPENS FOR A REASON?` → `SOMETIMES A SLAP.` → `WHAT DOES THE VERSE ACTUALLY SAY?`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose." First, what it doesn't say: that all things are good. Paul has just spent a paragraph on suffering, groaning, a world in labor pains. He's not pretending cancer is good, or cruelty, or loss. Second, what it does say. Work together is one word in Greek, synergei; you can hear our word synergy in it. Things that are not good in themselves are worked together, woven, into something good. A weaver uses dark threads as well as bright ones, and the pattern only shows from the other side. That picture isn't Paul's, but it helps with his word. And who does the working? The verse is about those who love God and are called according to his purpose, so some readers hear God as the subject: God works all things together for good. God is the weaver, not luck. Then verses twenty-nine and thirty trace a golden chain: those God foreknew, he predestined, called, justified and glorified. Christians read that chain differently. Reformed Christians, following Calvin, stress God's sovereign choice. Methodists and others, following Wesley, stress that God's foreknowledge leaves room for human freedom. Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds God's grace and human cooperation together. Each finds the same comfort in it: the story is held. And this week, peace with God, Adam and Christ, dead to sin, the wretched man, no condemnation, the groaning world, all gets woven together.
screen: `NOT: ALL THINGS ARE GOOD.` · `SYNERGEI: WOVEN TOGETHER.` · `GOD WORKS ALL THINGS TOGETHER.` · `A GOLDEN CHAIN, READ THREE WAYS.` · then, large: `ALL THINGS WORK TOGETHER FOR GOOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something hard, and don't call it good, it may not be; just turn it over gently, the way you'd turn a woven cloth to see the back, and look for one thread of good worked into it: a kindness, something you learned, a friend who showed up. If you can't find one yet, that's all right; Paul says we know, not that we always see. If you pray, hand the hard thing to God, the weaver.
Synergei. Paul's Greek word for worked together: not that hard things are good, but that even they get woven into good.
Your line: a good thread in the weave. Dark threads belong too. See you tomorrow.
